Reference: Shapiro (2025)

Model Setting

The paper proposes that strong institutions give a country comparative advantage in clean industries and thereby improve its environmental quality. This supply-side channel is set beside three established explanations of the global distribution of pollution: weak environmental regulation (the Pollution Havens Hypothesis), capital endowments that attract capital-intensive dirty industries (Heckscher-Ohlin), and income (the Environmental Kuznets Curve). Three institutions are studied: financial, judicial and labour market institutions. Five complementary tests are used. First, industries that depend on institutions are clean. Second, strong institutions raise relative exports of clean industries. Third, the complexity of an industry helps explain the link. Fourth, cross-country differences in the composition of output account for an important share of cross-country differences in emissions. Fifth, a quantitative general equilibrium trade model shows that strengthening a country's institutions lowers its own pollution by relocating dirty industries abroad, and raises pollution in other countries. Cost structure explains why institutions, which do not target pollution, can matter as much as environmental regulation: regulation raises the costs of the dirtiest industries by at most a few percent, whereas institutions change the productivity of intermediate goods and factors, which make up most of a firm's costs.

Country institutions are measured around 2012 in z-scores, with higher values denoting better institutions. Financial institutions are private credit by deposit money institutions relative to GDP, judicial institutions are the World Bank Rule of Law index, and labour market institutions are the Heritage Foundation labour market freedom index (flexibility of hiring, firing and hours). The institutions index is their first principal component. Environmental regulation is the first principal component of four of eight available measures (diesel sulphur standard, survey measures of stringency and of enforcement, number of environmental treaties). Factor endowments are the log capital stock per worker and the Penn World Tables human capital index. Industry variables come from about 350 US six-digit NAICS manufacturing industries in 2012. An industry's dependence on institutions is asset intangibility (one minus the share of property, plant and equipment in assets) for financial institutions, the share of inputs that are neither traded on open exchanges nor reference priced (Rauch 1999) for judicial institutions, and the employment-weighted standard deviation of within-firm sales growth for labour market institutions. The clean index is minus one times the first principal component of two emission rates: the air pollution rate (itself the first principal component of log emissions per dollar of revenue for carbon monoxide, nitrogen oxides, PM2.5, sulphur dioxide and volatile organic compounds) and log water pollution emissions per dollar of revenue. All environmental variables are scaled so that higher values mean better environmental quality. Bilateral trade comes from BACI (134 countries plus a rest-of-world region), applied tariffs from Macmap, and Exiobase 3.8.1 (163 industries) supplies output and air emissions by country and industry for the decomposition and the quantitative model.

Cross-Country and Cross-Industry Correlations

Two descriptive regressions motivate the analysis. Across countries iii:

Zi=ρ0C+ρ1CIi+ϵi(9.1.1.1)Z_i=\rho^C_0+\rho^C_1I_i+\epsilon_i \tag{9.1.1.1}Zi​=ρ0C​+ρ1C​Ii​+ϵi​(9.1.1.1)

and across industries sss:

Zs=ρ0I+ρ1IIs+ϵs(9.1.1.2)Z_s=\rho^I_0+\rho^I_1I_s+\epsilon_s \tag{9.1.1.2}Zs​=ρ0I​+ρ1I​Is​+ϵs​(9.1.1.2)

where ZiZ_iZi​ is ambient air or water quality in country iii (minus the log of mean PM2.5 or of biochemical oxygen demand), IiI_iIi​ is national institutional quality, ZsZ_sZs​ is the clean index of industry sss, and IsI_sIs​ is the dependence of industry sss on institutions. Neither regression is causal, and the first does not separate comparative advantage from other channels. Countries with stronger financial and judicial institutions have significantly better air and water quality, while the relationship for labour market institutions is not significant. Across industries, the binned scatter plots (which put dependence on the vertical axis and the clean index on the horizontal axis) have slopes of 0.58 for financial, 0.49 for judicial and 0.18 for labour market institutions, with R-squared of 0.34, 0.24 and 0.03. The five cleanest manufacturing industries have a mean institutional dependence index of 0.65 and the five dirtiest a mean of −1.47-1.47−1.47, a gap of 2.12 standard deviations. Fluid power pumps (clean index 2.42) depend more than average on all three institutions, and gypsum products (clean index −2.18-2.18−2.18) depend less on all three.

where Xij,sX_{ij,s}Xij,s​ is the value of trade from origin iii to destination jjj in industry sss, Ti,sT_{i,s}Ti,s​ is the technology level of the origin in that sector, ci,sc_{i,s}ci,s​ is the unit production cost, Xj,sX_{j,s}Xj,s​ is expenditure, Pj,sP_{j,s}Pj,s​ is the importer price index, ϕij,s\phi_{ij,s}ϕij,s​ is the full trade cost made up of iceberg costs τij,s≥1\tau_{ij,s}\geq1τij,s​≥1 and tariffs tij,st_{ij,s}tij,s​, θs\theta_sθs​ is the trade elasticity, and ξ\xiξ is a constant. The first line absorbs importer expenditure and prices in importer-by-industry fixed effects ζj,s\zeta_{j,s}ζj,s​. An interaction of the clean index with GDP per capita is not part of the baseline, because GDP is an endogenous outcome of all endowments in the model and a bad control in the regression.

Comparative Advantage in Clean Industries

If institutions provide comparative advantage and the industries that benefit are clean, institutions should provide comparative advantage in clean industries. The direct test replaces institutional dependence with the clean index:

ln⁡Xij,s=αCEiZs+∑fβfCEifIsf+πCRiZs+γCtij,s+ζj,sC+ηijC+ϵij,sC(9.1.1.7)\ln X_{ij,s}=\alpha^CE_iZ_s+\sum_f\beta^C_fE^f_iI^f_s+\pi^CR_iZ_s+\gamma^Ct_{ij,s}+\zeta^C_{j,s}+\eta^C_{ij}+\epsilon^C_{ij,s} \tag{9.1.1.7}lnXij,s​=αCEi​Zs​+f∑​βfC​Eif​Isf​+πCRi​Zs​+γCtij,s​+ζj,sC​+ηijC​+ϵij,sC​(9.1.1.7)

The country-pair fixed effects ηijC\eta^C_{ij}ηijC​ absorb the level effect of the exporter's institutions and the destination-by-sector fixed effects ζj,sC\zeta^C_{j,s}ζj,sC​ absorb the level effect of the clean index, so identification comes only from the interaction. A back-of-envelope calculation moves a country from the tenth to the ninetieth percentile of institutional quality. Baseline environmental quality is Zi=∑j,sXij,sZsZ_i=\sum_{j,s}X_{ij,s}Z_sZi​=∑j,s​Xij,s​Zs​ and the counterfactual value is, as printed in the paper:

where E0.9eE^e_{0.9}E0.9e​ and E0.1eE^e_{0.1}E0.1e​ are the ninetieth and tenth percentiles of institutional quality (means of the index between the eighty-fifth and ninety-fifth, and between the fifth and fifteenth, percentiles), and the reported effect is Zi′/Zi−1Z'_i/Z_i-1Zi′​/Zi​−1. The calculation is partial equilibrium, covers only traded manufacturing goods, holds all other determinants of specialization fixed and assumes log-linear effects; the quantitative model relaxes these assumptions.

Three concerns are that institutions are measured with error, are correlated with other country characteristics, and respond to trade and production. The paper compares fifteen measures of institutions, builds an index, instruments institutions with historical variables (legal origins, settler mortality, population density in 1500; reported in the supplementary appendix), and uses variation within countries over time and across states within a country. The panel version for years yyy from 1996 to 2015 is:

ln⁡Xij,sy=αPEi,yZs+∑fβfPEi,yfIsf+ζj,syP+ηij,yP+ϵij,syP(9.1.1.9)\ln X_{ij,sy}=\alpha^PE_{i,y}Z_s+\sum_f\beta^P_fE^f_{i,y}I^f_s+\zeta^P_{j,sy}+\eta^P_{ij,y}+\epsilon^P_{ij,sy} \tag{9.1.1.9}lnXij,sy​=αPEi,y​Zs​+f∑​βfP​Ei,yf​Isf​+ζj,syP​+ηij,yP​+ϵij,syP​(9.1.1.9)

where trade, institutions, factor endowments and both sets of fixed effects vary by year, while ZsZ_sZs​, IsfI^f_sIsf​ and tariffs are time-invariant. The parameter αP\alpha^PαP is identified from changes in institutional quality within a country, which removes time-invariant country characteristics such as geography. A long-difference version uses 2000 and 2015, which reduces attenuation from measurement error and allows trade to respond gradually. Between 1996 and 2015 the institutions of the mean country changed by half a standard deviation in absolute value, improving in about two thirds of countries. A second design uses gross output Xi,sX_{i,s}Xi,s​ of industry sss in Indian state iii (26 states with data, 2015-2016 Annual Survey of Industry):

with state fixed effects ηiI\eta^I_iηiI​ and industry fixed effects ζsI\zeta^I_sζsI​, which addresses unobserved country-level determinants of specialization.

Key Estimates

Each observation is an importer-exporter-manufacturing industry triple (1,875,532 observations), and all coefficients are standardized betas with standard errors in parentheses.

  • All industries: entered one at a time, the interaction of endowment and intensity has a coefficient of 0.057 (0.012) for financial institutions, 0.054 (0.010) for judicial institutions, 0.006 (0.004) for labour market institutions, 0.057 (0.007) for the institutions index, 0.048 (0.009) for environmental regulation, −0.025-0.025−0.025 (0.096) for capital per worker and 0.348 (0.036) for skills; the coefficient on log tariffs is −0.085-0.085−0.085 (0.009). In the pooled regression the index has 0.038 (0.008), environmental regulation 0.022 (0.009), capital 0.172 (0.098) and skills 0.285 (0.033).

  • Clean industries: the interaction of institutions with the clean index has a coefficient of 0.051 (0.010) for financial, 0.054 (0.010) for judicial and 0.018 (0.008) for labour market institutions, and 0.054 (0.007) for the index. With all controls the index has 0.038 (0.012) against 0.008 (0.014) for environmental regulation; when the three institutions enter together only financial institutions remain significant, at 0.035 (0.015).

  • Magnitudes: moving from the tenth to the ninetieth percentile of institutions lowers a country's emissions by 21.4 to 24.7 percent in the pooled specifications (14.8 to 38.1 percent one institution at a time). The institutions coefficient is just under half of the tariff coefficient, so for an industry one standard deviation cleaner than average, one standard deviation of institutions is worth a tariff cut of 4 to 7 percentage points.

  • Other designs: αP\alpha^PαP is 0.013 (0.005) in the full panel and 0.062 (0.031) in the long difference, against 0.038 (0.012) in the cross-section. The Indian estimates are moderately larger than the global baseline. When institutions are interacted with both the clean index and institutional dependence, the clean-index interaction mostly becomes small and insignificant, which supports the interpretation that clean industries gain because they depend on institutions.

Explanations

Why do clean industries depend on institutions? Dirty industries heat, pressurize and combust raw materials with large tangible assets (kilns, furnaces, cracking units) that serve as collateral, so they need financial institutions less. Their inputs are homogeneous commodities traded on open exchanges, so they need courts to enforce bilateral contracts less. Their products face inelastic short-run supply and demand, so sales are less volatile and flexible hiring and firing matters less. The formal content is three regressions on an industry characteristic WsW_sWs​. The first asks which characteristics are correlated with being clean:

Zs=ρ0W+ρ1WWs+ϵsW(9.1.1.11)Z_s=\rho^W_0+\rho^W_1W_s+\epsilon^W_s \tag{9.1.1.11}Zs​=ρ0W​+ρ1W​Ws​+ϵsW​(9.1.1.11)

The second asks how controlling for WsW_sWs​ changes the association between the clean index and institutional dependence:

Zs=ρ0IW+ρ1IWIs+ρ2IWWs+ϵsIW(9.1.1.12)Z_s=\rho^{IW}_0+\rho^{IW}_1I_s+\rho^{IW}_2W_s+\epsilon^{IW}_s \tag{9.1.1.12}Zs​=ρ0IW​+ρ1IW​Is​+ρ2IW​Ws​+ϵsIW​(9.1.1.12)

The third adds the interaction of WsW_sWs​ with institutional quality to the clean-industry trade regression:

ln⁡Xij,s=αWEiZs+αWEiWs+∑fβfWEifIsf+πWRiZs+γWtij,s+ζj,sW+ηijW+ϵij,sW(9.1.1.13)\ln X_{ij,s}=\alpha^WE_iZ_s+\alpha^WE_iW_s+\sum_f\beta^W_fE^f_iI^f_s+\pi^WR_iZ_s+\gamma^Wt_{ij,s}+\zeta^W_{j,s}+\eta^W_{ij}+\epsilon^W_{ij,s} \tag{9.1.1.13}lnXij,s​=αWEi​Zs​+αWEi​Ws​+f∑​βfW​Eif​Isf​+πWRi​Zs​+γWtij,s​+ζj,sW​+ηijW​+ϵij,sW​(9.1.1.13)

where the paper uses the same symbol αW\alpha^WαW for both interaction coefficients and the object of interest is the first. Clean industries have lower energy shares (−0.37-0.37−0.37), raw materials shares (−0.36-0.36−0.36), upstreamness (−0.33-0.33−0.33) and log shipping costs per ton-kilometer (−0.41-0.41−0.41), and higher inverse export supply elasticities (0.27), labour shares (0.29) and college shares (0.18). No single characteristic removes the association between the clean index and institutional dependence, but all eighteen together reduce it from 0.58 to 0.17 (financial), from 0.49 to 0.17 (judicial) and from 0.18 to 0.06 (labour). In the trade regression the coefficient on the clean-index interaction falls from 0.041 (0.010) to 0.033 (0.007) with all controls, and the paper states that the controls together account for about 25 percent of the comparative advantage. The most important variables describe clean industries as specialized, skilled and downstream, that is, complex.

Scale, Composition and Technique

Earlier decompositions within a country over time find that technique, not composition, drives pollution, which seems to leave little room for comparative advantage. The paper applies the same decomposition across countries in a cross-section. Let E\mathcal{E}E be a country's total emissions, Es\mathcal{E}_sEs​ the emissions of industry sss, xsx_sxs​ its sales, es=Es/xse_s=\mathcal{E}_s/x_ses​=Es​/xs​ its emissions intensity, XXX total sales and κs\kappa_sκs​ the share of industry sss in sales:

E=∑sEs=∑sxses=X∑sκses(9.1.1.14)\mathcal{E}=\sum_s\mathcal{E}_s=\sum_sx_se_s=X\sum_s\kappa_se_s \tag{9.1.1.14}E=s∑​Es​=s∑​xs​es​=Xs∑​κs​es​(9.1.1.14)

Total differentiation gives:

dE=κ′edX+Xe′dκ+Xκ′de(9.1.1.15)d\mathcal{E}=\kappa'\mathbf{e}dX+X\mathbf{e}'d\kappa+X\kappa'd\mathbf{e} \tag{9.1.1.15}dE=κ′edX+Xe′dκ+Xκ′de(9.1.1.15)

where the three terms are the scale, composition and technique effects. Instead of projecting emission rates of a reference year onto later years, the paper projects the emission rates of a reference country rrr onto each focal country iii:

Scalei,r=∑sxis∑sxrs(9.1.1.16)\text{Scale}_{i,r}=\frac{\sum_sx_{is}}{\sum_sx_{rs}} \tag{9.1.1.16}Scalei,r​=∑s​xrs​∑s​xis​​(9.1.1.16)
Compositioni,r=∑sκisers∑sκrsers=∑sκisersZr/Xr(9.1.1.17)\text{Composition}_{i,r}=\frac{\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{rs}}{\sum_s\kappa_{rs}e_{rs}}=\frac{\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{rs}}{Z_r/X_r} \tag{9.1.1.17}Compositioni,r​=∑s​κrs​ers​∑s​κis​ers​​=Zr​/Xr​∑s​κis​ers​​(9.1.1.17)
Techniquei,r=∑sκiseis∑sκisers=Zi/Xi∑sκisers(9.1.1.18)\text{Technique}_{i,r}=\frac{\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{is}}{\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{rs}}=\frac{Z_i/X_i}{\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{rs}} \tag{9.1.1.18}Techniquei,r​=∑s​κis​ers​∑s​κis​eis​​=∑s​κis​ers​Zi​/Xi​​(9.1.1.18)

where xisx_{is}xis​ is gross output of country iii in industry sss, κis\kappa_{is}κis​ its share in the country's gross output and eise_{is}eis​ emissions per dollar of gross output; in the last two expressions Zr/XrZ_r/X_rZr​/Xr​ and Zi/XiZ_i/X_iZi​/Xi​ stand for aggregate emissions per dollar of gross output. Composition weights output shares by reference emission rates and technique holds shares at the focal country's values, as in the time-series literature (the derivation is in the supplementary appendix). Each term is reported minus one, as a proportional difference from the reference country. Because effects differ in sign across countries, relative importance is summarized by:

∣Composition∣∣Composition∣+∣Technique∣(9.1.1.19)\frac{|\text{Composition}|}{|\text{Composition}|+|\text{Technique}|} \tag{9.1.1.19}∣Composition∣+∣Technique∣∣Composition∣​(9.1.1.19)

For sulphur oxides, India produces 87 percent less output than the US but emits 12 percent more; composition raises Indian emissions by 162 percent and technique by 216 percent, so composition accounts for 43 percent. With the US as reference and all pollutants pooled, the mean country has 72 percent lower emissions and 89 percent lower output, a composition effect of 1.75 and a technique effect of −0.02-0.02−0.02; the mean absolute effects are 1.76 and 0.47, so composition accounts for 79 percent. Across all country pairs the mean and median share are about 0.70, and 0.63 among high-income countries with directly reported emissions. Reference-country fixed effects explain 37 percent of the variation in the share, focal-country fixed effects 14 percent and both 50 percent. Composition therefore matters at least as much as technique in the cross-section, plausibly because abatement technology can cut a source's emissions by more than 95 percent almost immediately while institutions persist, and because technique depends on absolute emission rates while composition depends on relative comparative advantage.

Quantitative Model

The model is a multi-country, multi-sector structural gravity model with pollution (Costinot and Rodriguez-Clare 2014; Shapiro 2021), with intermediate goods, input-output links, trade imbalances, tariffs and emission rates for every country and industry in all sectors of the economy. Each country has a representative agent whose utility is a constant elasticity of substitution aggregate across varieties and Cobb-Douglas across sectors, and who suffers disutility from pollution. Markets are perfectly competitive as in Eaton and Kortum (2002): buyers source each variety from the lowest-price producer, and trade faces iceberg costs and tariffs. Production is Cobb-Douglas in labour and intermediate goods, which combine inputs from all sectors according to an input-output table. Productivity is Frechet distributed with location parameter Ti,sT_{i,s}Ti,s​ and dispersion parameter θs\theta_sθs​. All firms within a country and industry have the same emissions intensity, so a single elasticity governs how pollution responds to institutions.

Institutions enter only through productivity, potentially in every sector including non-tradables. Writing x^=x′/x\hat{x}=x'/xx^=x′/x for the proportional change of any variable xxx, the productivity equation implies that moving institutions from EiE_iEi​ to Ei′E'_iEi′​ changes productivity by:

T^i,s=exp⁡{αIs(Ei′−Ei)}(9.1.1.20)\hat{T}_{i,s}=\exp\left\{\alpha I_s\left(E'_i-E_i\right)\right\} \tag{9.1.1.20}T^i,s​=exp{αIs​(Ei′​−Ei​)}(9.1.1.20)

Because IsI_sIs​ is a z-score, better institutions raise productivity in industries with above-average dependence and lower it in industries with below-average dependence. The counterfactuals therefore abstract from any effect of institutions that is uniform across industries and capture only comparative advantage. Emissions of country iii are:

Ei=∑sγi,sRi,sci,s(9.1.1.21)\mathcal{E}_i=\sum_s\frac{\gamma_{i,s}R_{i,s}}{c_{i,s}} \tag{9.1.1.21}Ei​=s∑​ci,s​γi,s​Ri,s​​(9.1.1.21)

where γi,s\gamma_{i,s}γi,s​ is baseline pollution per real dollar of revenue, Ri,sR_{i,s}Ri,s​ is revenue and ci,sc_{i,s}ci,s​ is the unit cost, which serves as the deflator so that Ri,s/ci,sR_{i,s}/c_{i,s}Ri,s​/ci,s​ measures the quantity and not the value of output. The intensity γi,s\gamma_{i,s}γi,s​ is held fixed in counterfactuals, on the grounds that the estimated effect of institutions on technique within industries is muted; if better institutions also made techniques cleaner, the model would understate their environmental benefits.

In the competitive equilibrium, utility maximization yields the gravity equation above, and expenditure Xj,sX_{j,s}Xj,s​ equals spending on final plus intermediate goods, with income that includes fixed trade deficits and tariff revenue. Counterfactuals are computed in changes with exact hat algebra (Dekle, Eaton and Kortum 2008): given baseline trade and production data, trade elasticities and the shocks T^i,s\hat{T}_{i,s}T^i,s​, the system is solved for the changes in costs, prices, trade shares and revenues without recovering the levels of technology or trade costs. The full set of equilibrium conditions and the system in changes are in the supplementary appendix and are not reproduced in the main text, which reports only the resulting change in pollution:

E^i=∑s(R^i,s/c^i,s)Ei,s∑sEi,s(9.1.1.22)\hat{\mathcal{E}}_i=\frac{\sum_s\left(\hat{R}_{i,s}/\hat{c}_{i,s}\right)\mathcal{E}_{i,s}}{\sum_s\mathcal{E}_{i,s}} \tag{9.1.1.22}E^i​=∑s​Ei,s​∑s​(R^i,s​/c^i,s​)Ei,s​​(9.1.1.22)

where Ei,s\mathcal{E}_{i,s}Ei,s​ is baseline pollution of country iii in sector sss. The change in a country's pollution is the baseline-emissions-weighted mean of changes in real sectoral output.

Calibration

The model is applied to Exiobase trade, production and air pollution data aggregated to 10 regions (Pacific Ocean, Western Europe, Eastern Europe, Latin America, North America, China, Southern Europe, Northern Europe, Indian Ocean, Rest of World) and 21 industries; with finer aggregation the solution algorithm does not always converge. The trade elasticities θs\theta_sθs​ are sector-specific averages across four studies (Caliendo and Parro 2015; Shapiro 2016; Giri, Yi and Yilmazkuday 2020; Bagwell, Staiger and Yurukoglu 2021) and range from 2.99 to 13.53. The only other estimated parameter is α\alphaα, taken from the gravity regression for all industries, combined with data on IsI_sIs​ and EiE_iEi​; a counterfactual is defined by choosing Ei′E'_iEi′​. Baseline expenditure shares, input-output shares, deficits, tariffs and emissions Ei,s\mathcal{E}_{i,s}Ei,s​ are read from the data. The regressions thus have a model-based interpretation: they estimate how institutions shift the fundamental productivity Ti,sT_{i,s}Ti,s​.

Counterfactuals

Baseline institutional quality (z-score) is highest in North America (2.4), Northern Europe (2.2) and the Pacific Ocean (1.9), and lowest in Latin America (−0.6-0.6−0.6) and the Indian Ocean (−0.3-0.3−0.3).

  • One standard deviation, one region at a time: emissions in the reforming region fall by 3.9 percent (North America, Indian Ocean) to 7.8 percent (Northern Europe), with 5.9 percent for China. Emissions in every other region rise, by up to 1.3 percent, and more in regions that are close trading partners (Northern Europe when Western Europe reforms, the Pacific Ocean when China reforms) or when the reforming region is large. Global emissions change by between −1.5-1.5−1.5 percent (China) and +0.3+0.3+0.3 percent (Pacific Ocean): they fall when regions with dirty techniques reform and rise when regions with clean techniques reform.

  • Equalizing institutions at the global mean: emissions rise by 10.6 percent in Northern Europe, 6.5 percent in North America and 6.2 percent in the Pacific Ocean, and fall by 8.9 percent in Latin America, 6.8 percent in the Rest of World and 4.8 percent in the Indian Ocean; global emissions fall by 2.3 percent. In Latin America the output share of the dirtiest third of industries falls by 1.1 percent and that of the cleanest third rises by 2.1 percent.

  • Raising below-median regions to the mean of above-median regions: institutions improve by 1.1 to 2.4 standard deviations in the five targeted regions, whose emissions fall by 5.3 percent (China) to 9.6 percent (Latin America). Emissions in the five untargeted regions rise by 2.5 to 4.0 percent, and global emissions fall by 4.3 percent.

  • Latin America to the strongest region: an improvement of 3.1 standard deviations lowers Latin American emissions by 14.2 percent (the text describes this as nearly 20 percent), with the dirty, moderate and clean output shares changing by −1.8-1.8−1.8, −1.4-1.4−1.4 and +3.2+3.2+3.2 percent. Emissions elsewhere rise by 0.1 to 0.9 percent, the most in North America, and global emissions fall by 0.7 percent.

  • Observed changes from 1996 to 2015: institutions improved most in China (0.8), Northern Europe (0.6) and Eastern Europe (0.5), lowering their emissions by 4.8, 4.0 and 1.6 percent; they deteriorated in the Indian Ocean (−0.2-0.2−0.2), where emissions rise by 1.3 percent. Global emissions fall by 1.4 percent.

  • Interpretation: reforms mainly reallocate dirty production across countries. Global emissions fall modestly because dirty industries have lower emission intensities where baseline institutions are strong, but general equilibrium relocation dampens the global effect implied by the reduced-form regressions. Composition effects are therefore most relevant for explaining or lowering one country's emissions, and technique remains the main lever for global emissions.

This is a descriptive regression across countries iii. The outcome ZiZ_iZi​ is ambient environmental quality, measured as minus the log of mean PM2.5 (air) or minus the log of biochemical oxygen demand (water), so a higher value means a cleaner environment. The regressor IiI_iIi​ is national institutional quality in z-score units (financial, judicial or labour market institutions, or their index); it is the same object that the gravity equations later call EiE_iEi​. The intercept is ρ0C\rho^C_0ρ0C​, and ϵi\epsilon_iϵi​ collects everything else that moves pollution.

Because the outcome is minus a log and the regressor is a z-score, the slope is a semi-elasticity:

ρ1C=Cov⁡(Zi,Ii)Var⁡(Ii),∂ln⁡(pollutioni)∂Ii=−ρ1C\rho^C_1=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Z_i,I_i)}{\operatorname{Var}(I_i)},\qquad\frac{\partial\ln\left(\text{pollution}_i\right)}{\partial I_i}=-\rho^C_1ρ1C​=Var(Ii​)Cov(Zi​,Ii​)​,∂Ii​∂ln(pollutioni​)​=−ρ1C​

As an illustration, ρ1C=0.3\rho^C_1=0.3ρ1C​=0.3 would mean that a country whose institutions are one standard deviation stronger has ambient pollution lower by the factor e−0.3≈0.74e^{-0.3}\approx0.74e−0.3≈0.74, that is, about 26 percent lower.

The regression is not causal. Institutions are correlated with income, environmental regulation and factor endowments, all of which sit in ϵi\epsilon_iϵi​. Even a causal slope would pool every channel through which institutions matter: the scale of output, the composition of output across industries and the technique used within industries, which are the three terms of equation (15). The paper is interested in the composition channel alone, and a country-level regression cannot isolate it. That is the task of the interaction regressions (6) and (7), where anything that varies only by country is absorbed by fixed effects and only the differential effect across industries is used. Note also that the symbol ZiZ_iZi​ is reused with a different meaning in equation (8), where it is a trade-weighted clean index of a country's exports and not ambient quality.

This is the industry-level counterpart of equation (1). The unit is one of about 350 US six-digit manufacturing industries sss. The variable ZsZ_sZs​ is the clean index (minus the first principal component of log air and water emissions per dollar of revenue, so higher is cleaner) and IsI_sIs​ is the industry's dependence on financial, judicial or labour market institutions.

Both variables are z-scores, which gives the slope a simple reading. With unit variances,

ρ1I=Cov⁡(Zs,Is)Var⁡(Is)=Corr⁡(Zs,Is),R2=(ρ1I)2\rho^I_1=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Z_s,I_s)}{\operatorname{Var}(I_s)}=\operatorname{Corr}(Z_s,I_s),\qquad R^2=\left(\rho^I_1\right)^2ρ1I​=Var(Is​)Cov(Zs​,Is​)​=Corr(Zs​,Is​),R2=(ρ1I​)2

so the slope is the correlation coefficient and is the same whichever variable is placed on the left. This is why it does not matter that the paper's figure puts dependence on the vertical axis while the equation puts the clean index on the left. The reported numbers confirm it: 0.582≈0.340.58^2\approx0.340.582≈0.34, 0.492≈0.240.49^2\approx0.240.492≈0.24 and 0.182≈0.030.18^2\approx0.030.182≈0.03 are the reported R-squared values.

The regression supplies one of the two links in the paper's argument. Write the linear projection of dependence on the clean index as Is=ρ1IZs+usI_s=\rho^I_1Z_s+u_sIs​=ρ1I​Zs​+us​ and substitute it into the institutions term of the technology equation in (5):

αEiIs=αρ1IEiZs+αEius\alpha E_iI_s=\alpha\rho^I_1E_iZ_s+\alpha E_iu_sαEi​Is​=αρ1I​Ei​Zs​+αEi​us​

If institutions raise productivity in dependent industries (α>0\alpha>0α>0) and dependent industries are clean (ρ1I>0\rho^I_1>0ρ1I​>0), then institutions raise productivity in clean industries, with a coefficient of roughly αρ1I\alpha\rho^I_1αρ1I​ on EiZsE_iZ_sEi​Zs​. Equation (7) estimates that coefficient directly. The regression is a correlation, not a causal statement, and it relies on US data: the ranking of industries by cleanliness and by dependence is treated as a technological feature that carries over to other countries. Equations (11) and (12) ask which industry characteristics lie behind the correlation.

This is the sector-level Eaton-Kortum gravity equation. The derivation uses the assumptions listed in the Quantitative Model section of the note. Three remarks. First, Ti,sT_{i,s}Ti,s​ enters with exponent one while costs enter with exponent −θs-\theta_s−θs​, so the trade elasticity is the Frechet dispersion parameter and the substitution elasticity σs\sigma_sσs​ only affects the constant. Second, the constant depends on sss whenever θs\theta_sθs​ or σs\sigma_sσs​ does; the paper writes a single ξ\xiξ, which is harmless because any industry-specific constant is absorbed by the importer-by-industry fixed effect in equation (6). Third, since ϕij,s\phi_{ij,s}ϕij,s​ includes the tariff, Xij,sX_{ij,s}Xij,s​ here is spending inclusive of tariffs.

These are two definitions that close the gravity equation (3).

The first defines expenditure of destination jjj on industry sss as the sum of its purchases from all origins iii, including purchases from itself (i=ji=ji=j). It is an adding-up condition, and it pins down the price index. Summing equation (3) over iii and cancelling Xj,sX_{j,s}Xj,s​ gives

(Pj,s)−θs=ξ∑iTi,s(ci,sϕij,s)−θs\left(P_{j,s}\right)^{-\theta_s}=\xi\sum_iT_{i,s}\left(c_{i,s}\phi_{ij,s}\right)^{-\theta_s}(Pj,s​)−θs​=ξi∑​Ti,s​(ci,s​ϕij,s​)−θs​

so the price index is low where productive, low-cost and nearby suppliers are available. This is the same object as the term Φj,s\Phi_{j,s}Φj,s​ in the derivation of equation (3).

The second defines the full trade cost. The iceberg cost τij,s≥1\tau_{ij,s}\geq1τij,s​≥1 is a real resource cost: τij,s\tau_{ij,s}τij,s​ units must be shipped for one unit to arrive. The tariff tij,st_{ij,s}tij,s​ is ad valorem and is levied on top of it, so the delivered price is scaled by τij,s(1+tij,s)\tau_{ij,s}\left(1+t_{ij,s}\right)τij,s​(1+tij,s​). Unlike the iceberg cost, the tariff generates revenue for the importer, which matters for income in the quantitative model but not for the form of equation (3). In logs the two parts separate, and the trade elasticity applies to each:

A numerical illustration: with τij,s=1.2\tau_{ij,s}=1.2τij,s​=1.2 and tij,s=0.1t_{ij,s}=0.1tij,s​=0.1 the full cost is ϕij,s=1.32\phi_{ij,s}=1.32ϕij,s​=1.32, and with θs=5\theta_s=5θs​=5 a 10 percent tariff alone multiplies bilateral trade by 1.1−5≈0.621.1^{-5}\approx0.621.1−5≈0.62.

These four lines are assumptions, not results. They state how each piece of the log of the gravity equation (3) is represented by regressors, fixed effects and errors.

Line 1 defines the importer-by-industry fixed effect ζj,s\zeta_{j,s}ζj,s​ as the market-size and price term of the destination. It imposes nothing, because any function of the pair (j,s)(j,s)(j,s) is absorbed by a full set of dummies. The sign of the price term is plus. In equation (3) the price index is in the denominator with exponent −θs-\theta_s−θs​, so the term that appears after taking logs is

Because Ti,sT_{i,s}Ti,s​ enters equation (3) with exponent one, α\alphaα is directly the effect on log exports, which is what equation (20) relies on.

Line 3 collects the constant, the unit cost and the trade cost. This is an unstated restriction: cost differences across industries within an exporter must be uncorrelated with the interaction regressors.

The fixed effects show what identifies α\alphaα. Take two exporters iii and i′i'i′ and two industries sss and s′s's′ selling to the same destination jjj. Differencing across industries removes ηij\eta_{ij}ηij​, and differencing again across exporters removes ζj,s\zeta_{j,s}ζj,s​:

(ln⁡Xij,s−ln⁡Xij,s′)−(ln⁡Xi′j,s−ln⁡Xi′j,s′)=α(Ei−Ei′)(Is−Is′)+other terms\left(\ln X_{ij,s}-\ln X_{ij,s'}\right)-\left(\ln X_{i'j,s}-\ln X_{i'j,s'}\right)=\alpha\left(E_i-E_{i'}\right)\left(I_s-I_{s'}\right)+\text{other terms}(lnXij,s​−lnXij,s′​)−(lnXi′j,s​−lnXi′j,s′​)=α(Ei​−Ei′​)(Is​−Is′​)+other terms

So α\alphaα is identified by whether the exporter with better institutions sells relatively more of the more dependent industry in a common market. The level effect of institutions on all exports of a country drops out and is not identified.

This is the direct test of comparative advantage in clean industries. It is equation (6) with the institutions interaction EiIsE_iI_sEi​Is​ replaced by EiZsE_iZ_sEi​Zs​, the interaction of exporter institutions with the industry's clean index. The superscript CCC marks coefficients, fixed effects and error of this specification. The coefficient of interest is

αC=∂2ln⁡Xij,s∂Ei ∂Zs\alpha^C=\frac{\partial^2\ln X_{ij,s}}{\partial E_i\,\partial Z_s}αC=∂Ei​∂Zs​∂2lnXij,s​​

Identification is as in equation (6). The pair effect ηijC\eta^C_{ij}ηijC​ absorbs everything specific to the exporter, including the level of EiE_iEi​, and the destination-by-industry effect ζj,sC\zeta^C_{j,s}ζj,sC​ absorbs everything specific to the industry, including the level of ZsZ_sZs​. One inconsistency of notation: the tariff enters here in levels, γCtij,s\gamma^Ct_{ij,s}γCtij,s​, while equation (6) uses ln⁡(1+tij,s)\ln\left(1+t_{ij,s}\right)ln(1+tij,s​), which is what the gravity equation implies, and the row label in the paper's table is the log of one plus tariffs. The regression actually run therefore appears to use the log form, and the level form is a slip in the paper's equation (the two are close for small tariffs).

The tariff coefficient gives a yardstick. The institutions coefficient is just under half of the tariff coefficient in absolute value, for example 0.038/0.085≈0.450.038/0.085\approx0.450.038/0.085≈0.45, and one standard deviation of tariffs is 9 percentage points weighted by trade and 15 unweighted. Hence one standard deviation of institutions, for an industry one standard deviation cleaner than average, moves exports as much as a tariff cut of about 0.45×9≈40.45\times9\approx40.45×9≈4 to 0.45×15≈70.45\times15\approx70.45×15≈7 percentage points.

Two caveats on this reconstruction. The level effect of institutions on all of a country's exports is absorbed by ηijC\eta^C_{ij}ηijC​ and is held fixed here; a version that divides by total exports, ∑j,sXij,s′Zs/∑j,sXij,s′\sum_{j,s}X'_{ij,s}Z_s/\sum_{j,s}X'_{ij,s}∑j,s​Xij,s′​Zs​/∑j,s​Xij,s′​, would be invariant to it. This is the panel version of equation (7), for years yyy from 1996 to 2015. Trade Xij,syX_{ij,sy}Xij,sy​, institutions Ei,yE_{i,y}Ei,y​ and endowments Ei,yfE^f_{i,y}Ei,yf​ vary over time; the clean index ZsZ_sZs​ and the intensities IsfI^f_sIsf​ are fixed industry characteristics. The printed equation has no regulation interaction and no tariff term; the paper treats tariffs as time-invariant because data for the full panel are limited. The destination-by-industry-by-year effect ζj,syP\zeta^P_{j,sy}ζj,syP​ absorbs demand and prices in each market and year, and the pair-by-year effect ηij,yP\eta^P_{ij,y}ηij,yP​ absorbs anything specific to an exporter or a pair in a year, including the level of Ei,yE_{i,y}Ei,y​ and the business cycle.

The purpose is to remove time-invariant country characteristics, such as geography, that are correlated with institutions and favour clean industries. The paper states that αP\alpha^PαP is identified from changes in institutions within a country. As printed, however, the equation contains no exporter-by-industry (or pair-by-industry) effect, and without one the cross-sectional variation used in equation (7) would still contribute. Identification from within-country changes needs such an effect, written here as μij,s\mu_{ij,s}μij,s​, a symbol that is not in the note. The long-difference version makes this explicit. Taking the difference between 2015 and 2000 of the equation with μij,s\mu_{ij,s}μij,s​ added,

Δln⁡Xij,s=αPΔEi Zs+∑fβfPΔEif Isf+Δζj,sP+ΔηijP+Δϵij,sP\Delta\ln X_{ij,s}=\alpha^P\Delta E_i\,Z_s+\sum_f\beta^P_f\Delta E^f_i\,I^f_s+\Delta\zeta^P_{j,s}+\Delta\eta^P_{ij}+\Delta\epsilon^P_{ij,s}ΔlnXij,s​=αPΔEi​Zs​+f∑​βfP​ΔEif​Isf​+Δζj,sP​+ΔηijP​+Δϵij,sP​

so μij,s\mu_{ij,s}μij,s​ drops out, together with any time-invariant tariff, and αP\alpha^PαP is identified by whether countries whose institutions improved by more saw larger export growth in cleaner industries.

The pattern of estimates fits standard reasoning about panels. Year-to-year changes in an institutions index are small and noisy, so measurement error attenuates the within estimate (0.0130.0130.013) relative to the cross-section (0.0380.0380.038); trade also adjusts slowly. Differencing over fifteen years raises the signal relative to the noise and allows for adjustment, and the estimate rises to 0.0620.0620.062. The three numbers are therefore read as short-run, long-run and medium-run responses. The identifying assumption is that changes in institutions are not correlated with other changes that favour clean industries, conditional on the endowment interactions.

This specification moves the test inside one country. The unit is an industry sss in an Indian state iii (26 states), and the outcome Xi,sX_{i,s}Xi,s​ is gross output, not bilateral trade. The regressors mirror equation (6): state institutions EiE_iEi​ interacted with dependence IsI_sIs​, state endowments EifE^f_iEif​ with intensities IsfI^f_sIsf​, and state regulation RiR_iRi​ with the clean index ZsZ_sZs​. The superscript III marks the coefficients of this specification.

The link to the model comes from summing the gravity equation (3) over destinations. Ignoring the difference between tariff-inclusive spending and producer revenue,

Xi,s=∑jXij,s=Ti,s(ci,s)−θsMi,s,Mi,s≡ξ∑j(ϕij,s)−θs(Pj,s)θsXj,sX_{i,s}=\sum_jX_{ij,s}=T_{i,s}\left(c_{i,s}\right)^{-\theta_s}M_{i,s},\qquad M_{i,s}\equiv\xi\sum_j\left(\phi_{ij,s}\right)^{-\theta_s}\left(P_{j,s}\right)^{\theta_s}X_{j,s}Xi,s​=j∑​Xij,s​=Ti,s​(ci,s​)−θs​Mi,s​,Mi,s​≡ξj∑​(ϕij,s​)−θs​(Pj,s​)θs​Xj,s​

where Mi,sM_{i,s}Mi,s​ is the market access of state iii in industry sss, a symbol not used in the note. Taking logs and using the technology line of equation (5),

ln⁡Xi,s=αEiIs+∑fβfEifIsf+πRiZs+[ln⁡Mi,s−θsln⁡ci,s]+ωi,s\ln X_{i,s}=\alpha E_iI_s+\sum_f\beta_fE^f_iI^f_s+\pi R_iZ_s+\left[\ln M_{i,s}-\theta_s\ln c_{i,s}\right]+\omega_{i,s}lnXi,s​=αEi​Is​+f∑​βf​Eif​Isf​+πRi​Zs​+[lnMi,s​−θs​lnci,s​]+ωi,s​

The specification follows if the bracketed term is approximately the sum of a state component and an industry component, which the state effect ηiI\eta^I_iηiI​ and the industry effect ζsI\zeta^I_sζsI​ then absorb. This is reasonable within a country: states face the same external tariffs and similar demand for each industry, and a state's wage level and remoteness affect all its industries.

The advantage of the design is that national factors that could confound the cross-country estimates, such as national trade policy, the legal system, currency and culture, are held fixed, so identification comes from differences in institutional quality across states of one country. The limitations are the small number of states, the narrower range of institutional variation within a country, and the use of output, which also reflects local demand. The estimates are moderately larger than the global baseline.

This is the first of three regressions that ask why clean industries depend on institutions. The unit is an industry sss, ZsZ_sZs​ is the clean index and WsW_sWs​ is one additional industry characteristic at a time: energy share, raw materials share, upstreamness, shipping cost per ton-kilometer, inverse export supply elasticity, labour share, college share and others, eighteen in total. The regression is run separately for each characteristic.

It is a bivariate descriptive regression, so the slope is the covariance of the two variables divided by the variance of the regressor, and equals their correlation when WsW_sWs​ is standardized like the clean index:

ρ1W=Cov⁡(Zs,Ws)Var⁡(Ws)\rho^W_1=\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(Z_s,W_s)}{\operatorname{Var}(W_s)}ρ1W​=Var(Ws​)Cov(Zs​,Ws​)​

A negative value such as −0.37-0.37−0.37 for the energy share says that industries that spend more on energy are dirtier; a positive value such as 0.290.290.29 for the labour share says that labour-intensive industries are cleaner.

The purpose is to build a profile of clean industries. The characteristics with negative slopes describe industries that transform raw materials with heat and bulk transport, are upstream, and sell homogeneous heavy goods. Those with positive slopes describe industries that are skilled, labour-intensive and downstream. No causal claim is made: a characteristic qualifies as a candidate explanation of the link between cleanliness and institutional dependence only if it is correlated with the clean index here and also with dependence, which is what equation (12) examines. The same characteristics are then interacted with institutions in the trade regression (13).

This regression adds the characteristic WsW_sWs​ to the cross-industry regression (2) and asks how much of the association between the clean index ZsZ_sZs​ and institutional dependence IsI_sIs​ survives. The coefficient ρ1IW\rho^{IW}_1ρ1IW​ is the association between the two among industries with the same value of WsW_sWs​.

The link between this coefficient and the one in equation (2) is the omitted-variable formula. Let δ\deltaδ be the slope of a regression of WsW_sWs​ on IsI_sIs​. Then

ρ1I=ρ1IW+ρ2IW δ\rho^I_1=\rho^{IW}_1+\rho^{IW}_2\,\deltaρ1I​=ρ1IW​+ρ2IW​δ

so the coefficient falls when the control is added if WsW_sWs​ is related to the clean index and to dependence with matching signs. When all three variables are standardized, with pairwise correlations rZIr_{ZI}rZI​, rZWr_{ZW}rZW​ and rIWr_{IW}rIW​, the partial coefficient is

ρ1IW=rZI−rZW rIW1−rIW2\rho^{IW}_1=\frac{r_{ZI}-r_{ZW}\,r_{IW}}{1-r_{IW}^2}ρ1IW​=1−rIW2​rZI​−rZW​rIW​​

As a hypothetical illustration, with rZI=0.58r_{ZI}=0.58rZI​=0.58, rZW=−0.37r_{ZW}=-0.37rZW​=−0.37 and rIW=−0.4r_{IW}=-0.4rIW​=−0.4 the coefficient is (0.58−0.148)/0.84≈0.51(0.58-0.148)/0.84\approx0.51(0.58−0.148)/0.84≈0.51: a single characteristic that is moderately correlated with both variables removes only a small part of the association.

This is what the paper finds. No single characteristic removes the association, but all eighteen together reduce it from 0.58 to 0.17 for financial, from 0.49 to 0.17 for judicial and from 0.18 to 0.06 for labour market institutions. The reading is that most of the reason clean industries depend on institutions is captured by observable features that make an industry complex: specialized, skilled and downstream. The exercise is an accounting of correlations and does not show that any characteristic causes dependence. The characteristics are also correlated with each other, so the contribution of each one depends on which others are included.

This regression takes the mediation question of equation (12) to trade. It is the clean-industry regression (7) with one more interaction, EiWsE_iW_sEi​Ws​, of exporter institutions with the characteristic WsW_sWs​ (or with all eighteen characteristics at once). The fixed effects and the other controls are as in equation (7).

Two notational points. The paper prints the same symbol αW\alpha^WαW for the coefficients on EiZsE_iZ_sEi​Zs​ and on EiWsE_iW_sEi​Ws​. They are different parameters; writing the second as α~W\tilde{\alpha}^Wα~W, the relevant part of the equation is

αWEiZs+α~WEiWs\alpha^WE_iZ_s+\tilde{\alpha}^WE_iW_sαWEi​Zs​+α~WEi​Ws​

and the object of interest is the first, the comparative advantage in clean industries that remains once institutions are allowed to favour industries with characteristic WsW_sWs​. In addition, as in equation (7), the tariff is written in levels although the gravity derivation and the paper's table use the log of one plus the tariff.

The logic is the omitted-variable formula applied to interactions. If institutions favour clean industries because clean industries are complex, then EiZsE_iZ_sEi​Zs​ in equation (7) partly stands in for EiWsE_iW_sEi​Ws​, and adding the latter lowers the coefficient on the former by α~W\tilde{\alpha}^Wα~W times the slope of WsW_sWs​ on ZsZ_sZs​. The share of the comparative advantage accounted for by the controls is

1−αWαC1-\frac{\alpha^W}{\alpha^C}1−αCαW​

with αC\alpha^CαC estimated on the same sample without the extra interactions. With the reported coefficients this is 1−0.033/0.041≈0.201-0.033/0.041\approx0.201−0.033/0.041≈0.20; the paper describes the share as about 25 percent, so its figure is presumably based on unrounded or slightly different estimates. Either way most of the effect remains, which means that the eighteen characteristics explain much of the cross-industry correlation in equation (12) but a smaller part of the trade pattern. The caveats are the same as for any mediation exercise: the characteristics are measured with error and are not randomly assigned, so the remaining coefficient is not a clean estimate of a direct effect.

This is an accounting identity; each equality uses one definition. First, a country's emissions are the sum of the emissions of its industries:

E=∑sEs\mathcal{E}=\sum_s\mathcal{E}_sE=s∑​Es​

Second, emissions intensity is defined as emissions per dollar of sales, es≡Es/xse_s\equiv\mathcal{E}_s/x_ses​≡Es​/xs​, so Es=xses\mathcal{E}_s=x_se_sEs​=xs​es​ and

E=∑sxses\mathcal{E}=\sum_sx_se_sE=s∑​xs​es​

Third, define total sales and the sales share of each industry:

X≡∑sxs,κs≡xsX,∑sκs=1X\equiv\sum_sx_s,\qquad\kappa_s\equiv\frac{x_s}{X},\qquad\sum_s\kappa_s=1X≡s∑​xs​,κs​≡Xxs​​,s∑​κs​=1

Substituting xs=Xκsx_s=X\kappa_sxs​=Xκs​ and taking XXX out of the sum,

E=∑sXκses=X∑sκses\mathcal{E}=\sum_sX\kappa_se_s=X\sum_s\kappa_se_sE=s∑​Xκs​es​=Xs∑​κs​es​

In vector notation this is E=Xκ′e\mathcal{E}=X\kappa'\mathbf{e}E=Xκ′e. Emissions are the product of the size of the economy and its average emissions intensity E/X=∑sκses\mathcal{E}/X=\sum_s\kappa_se_sE/X=∑s​κs​es​, and the average intensity is a share-weighted mean of industry intensities. It can be high because dirty industries have large shares (composition) or because each industry is dirty (technique). The identity holds for any classification of industries, but the split between the two depends on how fine the classification is: differences within an industry category are counted as technique.

Start from equation (14) in vector form, E=Xκ′e=X∑sκses\mathcal{E}=X\kappa'\mathbf{e}=X\sum_s\kappa_se_sE=Xκ′e=X∑s​κs​es​, and treat XXX, the shares and the intensities as variables. Apply the product rule to each term XκsesX\kappa_se_sXκs​es​:

d(Xκses)=κses dX+Xes dκs+Xκs desd\left(X\kappa_se_s\right)=\kappa_se_s\,dX+Xe_s\,d\kappa_s+X\kappa_s\,de_sd(Xκs​es​)=κs​es​dX+Xes​dκs​+Xκs​des​

Sum over industries:

dE=(∑sκses)dX+X∑ses dκs+X∑sκs desd\mathcal{E}=\left(\sum_s\kappa_se_s\right)dX+X\sum_se_s\,d\kappa_s+X\sum_s\kappa_s\,de_sdE=(s∑​κs​es​)dX+Xs∑​es​dκs​+Xs∑​κs​des​

and write the sums as inner products:

dE=κ′edX+Xe′dκ+Xκ′ded\mathcal{E}=\kappa'\mathbf{e}dX+X\mathbf{e}'d\kappa+X\kappa'd\mathbf{e}dE=κ′edX+Xe′dκ+Xκ′de

The first term is the scale effect (more output at unchanged shares and intensities), the second the composition effect (shares change at unchanged intensities) and the third the technique effect (intensities change at unchanged shares).

The paper says the expression is obtained by differentiating and then dividing by E\mathcal{E}E, but the printed equation is not divided. Dividing by E=Xκ′e\mathcal{E}=X\kappa'\mathbf{e}E=Xκ′e gives the proportional form:

dEE=dXX+e′dκκ′e+κ′deκ′e\frac{d\mathcal{E}}{\mathcal{E}}=\frac{dX}{X}+\frac{\mathbf{e}'d\kappa}{\kappa'\mathbf{e}}+\frac{\kappa'd\mathbf{e}}{\kappa'\mathbf{e}}EdE​=XdX​+κ′ee′dκ​+κ′eκ′de​

Two remarks. Because shares sum to one, ∑sdκs=0\sum_sd\kappa_s=0∑s​dκs​=0, and the composition term can be written with intensities measured relative to the average eˉ≡κ′e\bar{e}\equiv\kappa'\mathbf{e}eˉ≡κ′e:

X∑ses dκs=X∑s(es−eˉ)dκsX\sum_se_s\,d\kappa_s=X\sum_s\left(e_s-\bar{e}\right)d\kappa_sXs∑​es​dκs​=Xs∑​(es​−eˉ)dκs​

so composition raises emissions only when output shifts towards industries with above-average intensity. And the decomposition is exact only for infinitesimal changes; for discrete differences, as between two countries, there are interaction terms, which equations (16) to (18) handle with an exact multiplicative decomposition.

Equations (16), (17) and (18) are the discrete, cross-country counterpart of equation (15). Write equation (14) for the focal country iii and for the reference country rrr, with Xi≡∑sxisX_i\equiv\sum_sx_{is}Xi​≡∑s​xis​ and Ei\mathcal{E}_iEi​ denoting total output and total emissions of country iii:

Ei=Xi∑sκiseis,Er=Xr∑sκrsers\mathcal{E}_i=X_i\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{is},\qquad\mathcal{E}_r=X_r\sum_s\kappa_{rs}e_{rs}Ei​=Xi​s∑​κis​eis​,Er​=Xr​s∑​κrs​ers​

Take the ratio, then multiply and divide by the mixed term ∑sκisers\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{rs}∑s​κis​ers​, the average intensity of an economy with the output shares of iii and the emission rates of rrr:

EiEr=XiXr×∑sκisers∑sκrsers×∑sκiseis∑sκisers\frac{\mathcal{E}_i}{\mathcal{E}_r}=\frac{X_i}{X_r}\times\frac{\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{rs}}{\sum_s\kappa_{rs}e_{rs}}\times\frac{\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{is}}{\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{rs}}Er​Ei​​=Xr​Xi​​×∑s​κrs​ers​∑s​κis​ers​​×∑s​κis​ers​∑s​κis​eis​​

The mixed term cancels between the second and third factors, so the identity is exact. The three factors are the scale, composition and technique terms, and the first is the target:

Scalei,r=XiXr=∑sxis∑sxrs\text{Scale}_{i,r}=\frac{X_i}{X_r}=\frac{\sum_sx_{is}}{\sum_sx_{rs}}Scalei,r​=Xr​Xi​​=∑s​xrs​∑s​xis​​

The scale term has a counterfactual reading. An economy with the size of iii but the shares and emission rates of rrr would emit

Xi∑sκrsers=Scalei,r×ErX_i\sum_s\kappa_{rs}e_{rs}=\text{Scale}_{i,r}\times\mathcal{E}_rXi​s∑​κrs​ers​=Scalei,r​×Er​

so the scale term is the ratio of emissions that would result from the difference in size alone. Taking logs of the three-way identity gives a sum, the discrete analogue of the proportional form of equation (15):

ln⁡EiEr=ln⁡Scalei,r+ln⁡Compositioni,r+ln⁡Techniquei,r\ln\frac{\mathcal{E}_i}{\mathcal{E}_r}=\ln\text{Scale}_{i,r}+\ln\text{Composition}_{i,r}+\ln\text{Technique}_{i,r}lnEr​Ei​​=lnScalei,r​+lnCompositioni,r​+lnTechniquei,r​

The paper reports each term minus one. India produces 87 percent less output than the US, so the scale ratio is about 0.130.130.13 and is reported as −0.87-0.87−0.87. The scale term uses output data only and is therefore the same for every pollutant.

The composition term is the second factor of the three-way identity derived for equation (16). To see what it measures, start from the reference country, whose emissions by equation (14) are Er=Xr∑sκrsers\mathcal{E}_r=X_r\sum_s\kappa_{rs}e_{rs}Er​=Xr​∑s​κrs​ers​, and change only its output shares to those of country iii, keeping its size and its emission rates. The hypothetical economy emits Xr∑sκisersX_r\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{rs}Xr​∑s​κis​ers​. The ratio of the two is

Compositioni,r=Xr∑sκisersXr∑sκrsers=∑sκisers∑sκrsers\text{Composition}_{i,r}=\frac{X_r\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{rs}}{X_r\sum_s\kappa_{rs}e_{rs}}=\frac{\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{rs}}{\sum_s\kappa_{rs}e_{rs}}Compositioni,r​=Xr​∑s​κrs​ers​Xr​∑s​κis​ers​​=∑s​κrs​ers​∑s​κis​ers​​

which is the first equality. For the second, the denominator is the aggregate emissions intensity of the reference country:

∑sκrsers=∑sxrsXrers=ErXr\sum_s\kappa_{rs}e_{rs}=\sum_s\frac{x_{rs}}{X_r}e_{rs}=\frac{\mathcal{E}_r}{X_r}s∑​κrs​ers​=s∑​Xr​xrs​​ers​=Xr​Er​​

The paper writes this as Zr/XrZ_r/X_rZr​/Xr​; in that expression ZrZ_rZr​ stands for the total emissions of country rrr, not for a clean index, so the paper's notation clashes with its own earlier use of the letter. Substituting gives

Compositioni,r=∑sκisersZr/Xr\text{Composition}_{i,r}=\frac{\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{rs}}{Z_r/X_r}Compositioni,r​=Zr​/Xr​∑s​κis​ers​​

The link to the composition term of equation (15) appears when the reported quantity, the ratio minus one, is written in terms of share differences. With eˉr≡∑sκrsers\bar{e}_r\equiv\sum_s\kappa_{rs}e_{rs}eˉr​≡∑s​κrs​ers​, and using the fact that the share differences sum to zero,

Compositioni,r−1=∑s(κis−κrs)erseˉr=∑s(κis−κrs)ers−eˉreˉr\text{Composition}_{i,r}-1=\frac{\sum_s\left(\kappa_{is}-\kappa_{rs}\right)e_{rs}}{\bar{e}_r}=\sum_s\left(\kappa_{is}-\kappa_{rs}\right)\frac{e_{rs}-\bar{e}_r}{\bar{e}_r}Compositioni,r​−1=eˉr​∑s​(κis​−κrs​)ers​​=s∑​(κis​−κrs​)eˉr​ers​−eˉr​​

This is the discrete version of e′dκ/κ′e\mathbf{e}'d\kappa/\kappa'\mathbf{e}e′dκ/κ′e: the term is positive when country iii has larger output shares than rrr in industries that are dirtier than average at the emission rates of rrr. Only the emission rates of the reference country are used, so the term reflects differences in what countries produce and not in how they produce it. Weighting share differences by reference rates makes it a Laspeyres-type index, the convention of the time-series literature, where the reference is a base year. For sulphur oxides in India relative to the US the term is 2.622.622.62, reported as an increase of 162 percent.

The technique term is the third factor of the three-way identity derived for equation (16). Start from the hypothetical economy used for equation (17), which has the output shares of country iii and the emission rates of the reference country rrr, with average intensity ∑sκisers\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{rs}∑s​κis​ers​. Now replace the emission rates by those of country iii, keeping the shares. The average intensity becomes ∑sκiseis\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{is}∑s​κis​eis​, and the ratio is

Techniquei,r=∑sκiseis∑sκisers\text{Technique}_{i,r}=\frac{\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{is}}{\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{rs}}Techniquei,r​=∑s​κis​ers​∑s​κis​eis​​

which is the first equality. For the second, the numerator is the actual aggregate intensity of country iii, by equation (14):

∑sκiseis=∑sxisXieis=EiXi\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{is}=\sum_s\frac{x_{is}}{X_i}e_{is}=\frac{\mathcal{E}_i}{X_i}s∑​κis​eis​=s∑​Xi​xis​​eis​=Xi​Ei​​

which the paper writes as Zi/XiZ_i/X_iZi​/Xi​, with ZiZ_iZi​ again meaning total emissions. Hence

Techniquei,r=Zi/Xi∑sκisers\text{Technique}_{i,r}=\frac{Z_i/X_i}{\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{rs}}Techniquei,r​=∑s​κis​ers​Zi​/Xi​​

The reported quantity, the ratio minus one, is a weighted mean of industry-level differences in emission rates:

Techniquei,r−1=∑sκis(eis−ers)∑sκisers=∑sws(eisers−1),ws≡κisers∑s′κis′ers′\text{Technique}_{i,r}-1=\frac{\sum_s\kappa_{is}\left(e_{is}-e_{rs}\right)}{\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{rs}}=\sum_sw_s\left(\frac{e_{is}}{e_{rs}}-1\right),\qquad w_s\equiv\frac{\kappa_{is}e_{rs}}{\sum_{s'}\kappa_{is'}e_{rs'}}Techniquei,r​−1=∑s​κis​ers​∑s​κis​(eis​−ers​)​=s∑​ws​(ers​eis​​−1),ws​≡∑s′​κis′​ers′​κis​ers​​

This is the discrete version of κ′de/κ′e\kappa'd\mathbf{e}/\kappa'\mathbf{e}κ′de/κ′e in equation (15), with weights at the shares of the focal country (a Paasche-type index). It is positive when the same industries emit more per dollar in iii than in rrr.

The three terms multiply to the emissions ratio because the mixed term cancels and the two aggregate intensities remain:

Scalei,r×Compositioni,r×Techniquei,r=XiXr×∑sκisersEr/Xr×Ei/Xi∑sκisers=EiEr\text{Scale}_{i,r}\times\text{Composition}_{i,r}\times\text{Technique}_{i,r}=\frac{X_i}{X_r}\times\frac{\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{rs}}{\mathcal{E}_r/X_r}\times\frac{\mathcal{E}_i/X_i}{\sum_s\kappa_{is}e_{rs}}=\frac{\mathcal{E}_i}{\mathcal{E}_r}Scalei,r​×Compositioni,r​×Techniquei,r​=Xr​Xi​​×Er​/Xr​∑s​κis​ers​​×∑s​κis​ers​Ei​/Xi​​=Er​Ei​​

A check with the numbers for sulphur oxides in India relative to the US: 0.13×2.62×3.16≈1.080.13\times2.62\times3.16\approx1.080.13×2.62×3.16≈1.08, against a reported emissions ratio of 1.121.121.12; the gap is rounding in the output figure (a scale ratio of 0.1350.1350.135 gives 1.121.121.12). The reported terms minus one do not add up, because the decomposition is multiplicative. It is also not unique: weighting composition by the rates of iii and technique by the shares of rrr gives another exact split with different values, the usual index-number problem. The paper follows the convention of the time-series literature.

This is a summary statistic for the relative importance of the composition and technique terms of equations (17) and (18). Inside the absolute values are the terms as reported, that is, the ratios minus one, so each is a proportional difference in emissions relative to the reference country. The statistic lies between zero and one: one half means the two effects have the same magnitude, values above one half mean composition accounts for more.

Absolute values are needed because the effects take both signs. A country can be cleaner than the reference through composition and dirtier through technique, and across countries positive and negative values cancel in a mean. The table for the US as reference shows this: the mean technique effect is −0.02-0.02−0.02 while the mean absolute technique effect is 0.470.470.47. Two computations from the note:

1.621.62+2.16≈0.43,1.761.76+0.47≈0.79\frac{1.62}{1.62+2.16}\approx0.43,\qquad\frac{1.76}{1.76+0.47}\approx0.791.62+2.161.62​≈0.43,1.76+0.471.76​≈0.79

The first is sulphur oxides in India relative to the US; the second uses mean absolute effects across countries for all pollutants pooled. Across all country pairs the statistic is computed pair by pair and its mean and median are about 0.700.700.70.

Three caveats follow from the construction. The statistic is not a variance decomposition: since the terms of equations (16) to (18) multiply, the two absolute values do not sum to the total difference in emissions. It is not symmetric in the choice of reference country, because a proportional difference is bounded below by −1-1−1 and unbounded above (a ratio of 2 gives +1+1+1, the inverse ratio of 0.50.50.5 gives −0.5-0.5−0.5); a version in logs, ∣ln⁡Composition∣/(∣ln⁡Composition∣+∣ln⁡Technique∣)|\ln\text{Composition}|/(|\ln\text{Composition}|+|\ln\text{Technique}|)∣lnComposition∣/(∣lnComposition∣+∣lnTechnique∣), would be symmetric. And it depends on industry aggregation, since differences within one of the 163 industry categories are counted as technique. The use in the paper is qualitative: composition matters at least as much as technique in the cross-section, in contrast with the time-series literature, which leaves room for comparative advantage to shape a country's pollution.

Start from the technology line of equation (5), written for the baseline and for a counterfactual in which only the institutions of country iii change, from EiE_iEi​ to Ei′E'_iEi′​. Factor endowments, regulation and the unobserved component ωi,s\omega_{i,s}ωi,s​ are held fixed:

ln⁡Ti,s=αEiIs+∑fβfEifIsf+πRiZs+ωi,sln⁡Ti,s′=αEi′Is+∑fβfEifIsf+πRiZs+ωi,s\begin{aligned} \ln T_{i,s}&=\alpha E_iI_s+\sum_f\beta_fE^f_iI^f_s+\pi R_iZ_s+\omega_{i,s}\\ \ln T'_{i,s}&=\alpha E'_iI_s+\sum_f\beta_fE^f_iI^f_s+\pi R_iZ_s+\omega_{i,s} \end{aligned}lnTi,s​lnTi,s′​​=αEi​Is​+f∑​βf​Eif​Isf​+πRi​Zs​+ωi,s​=αEi′​Is​+f∑​βf​Eif​Isf​+πRi​Zs​+ωi,s​​

Subtract the first line from the second; everything except the institutions term cancels:

ln⁡Ti,s′−ln⁡Ti,s=αIs(Ei′−Ei)\ln T'_{i,s}-\ln T_{i,s}=\alpha I_s\left(E'_i-E_i\right)lnTi,s′​−lnTi,s​=αIs​(Ei′​−Ei​)

Exponentiate and use the definition T^i,s=Ti,s′/Ti,s\hat{T}_{i,s}=T'_{i,s}/T_{i,s}T^i,s​=Ti,s′​/Ti,s​:

T^i,s=exp⁡{αIs(Ei′−Ei)}\hat{T}_{i,s}=\exp\left\{\alpha I_s\left(E'_i-E_i\right)\right\}T^i,s​=exp{αIs​(Ei′​−Ei​)}

The levels Ti,sT_{i,s}Ti,s​ and the unobserved ωi,s\omega_{i,s}ωi,s​ are never needed, which is what makes the shock usable in exact hat algebra.

Three implications. First, the shock is a pure comparative-advantage shock. For two industries sss and s′s's′ in the same country,

T^i,sT^i,s′=exp⁡{α(Is−Is′)(Ei′−Ei)}\frac{\hat{T}_{i,s}}{\hat{T}_{i,s'}}=\exp\left\{\alpha\left(I_s-I_{s'}\right)\left(E'_i-E_i\right)\right\}T^i,s′​T^i,s​​=exp{α(Is​−Is′​)(Ei′​−Ei​)}

Because IsI_sIs​ is a z-score with mean zero, an improvement in institutions gives T^i,s>1\hat{T}_{i,s}>1T^i,s​>1 for industries with Is>0I_s>0Is​>0 and T^i,s<1\hat{T}_{i,s}<1T^i,s​<1 for industries with Is<0I_s<0Is​<0. A uniform effect of institutions on all industries would be absorbed by ηij\eta_{ij}ηij​ in equation (6); it is not identified and is set to zero here. Second, the regression coefficient can be used without rescaling by the trade elasticity: by equation (3), at given costs and price indices, X^ij,s=T^i,s\hat{X}_{ij,s}=\hat{T}_{i,s}X^ij,s​=T^i,s​, so α\alphaα is the effect on log exports per unit of EiIsE_iI_sEi​Is​, exactly what equation (6) estimates. In terms of the level of productivity, which is proportional to Ti,s1/θsT_{i,s}^{1/\theta_s}Ti,s1/θs​​ under the Frechet assumption, the change is

T^i,s1/θs=exp⁡{αθsIs(Ei′−Ei)}\hat{T}_{i,s}^{1/\theta_s}=\exp\left\{\frac{\alpha}{\theta_s}I_s\left(E'_i-E_i\right)\right\}T^i,s1/θs​​=exp{θs​α​Is​(Ei′​−Ei​)}

so the same shift in comparative advantage corresponds to a smaller change in physical productivity where the trade elasticity is high. Third, α\alphaα must be expressed in log points per unit of EiIsE_iI_sEi​Is​; the note reports standardized betas, which have to be converted to that scale. The functional form is log-linear, so large counterfactual changes, such as 3.1 standard deviations, extrapolate the regression well beyond marginal changes.

The equation combines an accounting step with an assumption about what generates pollution. The paper states the formula and describes ci,sc_{i,s}ci,s​ as the deflator; the reading of Ri,s/ci,sR_{i,s}/c_{i,s}Ri,s​/ci,s​ as a quantity of input bundles below is my own reconstruction.

Step 1. In the model, production has constant returns and markets are perfectly competitive, so every variety is sold at unit cost and there are no profits. Let Bi,sB_{i,s}Bi,s​ denote the number of input bundles (the Cobb-Douglas composite of labour and intermediate goods) used by industry sss in country iii, a symbol not in the note. Each bundle costs ci,sc_{i,s}ci,s​, so revenue equals cost:

Ri,s=ci,sBi,s⟹Bi,s=Ri,sci,sR_{i,s}=c_{i,s}B_{i,s}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad B_{i,s}=\frac{R_{i,s}}{c_{i,s}}Ri,s​=ci,s​Bi,s​⟹Bi,s​=ci,s​Ri,s​​

The ratio is a real quantity: if all prices double, revenue and unit cost both double and the ratio is unchanged.

Step 2. Assume that all firms in a country and industry have the same emissions intensity and that pollution is proportional to this real scale of activity, with factor γi,s\gamma_{i,s}γi,s​:

Ei,s=γi,sBi,s=γi,sRi,sci,s\mathcal{E}_{i,s}=\gamma_{i,s}B_{i,s}=\frac{\gamma_{i,s}R_{i,s}}{c_{i,s}}Ei,s​=γi,s​Bi,s​=ci,s​γi,s​Ri,s​​

Step 3. Sum over the sectors of the country:

Ei=∑sEi,s=∑sγi,sRi,sci,s\mathcal{E}_i=\sum_s\mathcal{E}_{i,s}=\sum_s\frac{\gamma_{i,s}R_{i,s}}{c_{i,s}}Ei​=s∑​Ei,s​=s∑​ci,s​γi,s​Ri,s​​

The parameter is calibrated by inverting Step 2 at the baseline:

γi,s=Ei,s ci,sRi,s\gamma_{i,s}=\frac{\mathcal{E}_{i,s}\,c_{i,s}}{R_{i,s}}γi,s​=Ri,s​Ei,s​ci,s​​

With baseline unit costs normalized to one, which is innocuous because only changes are computed, γi,s\gamma_{i,s}γi,s​ is observed pollution per dollar of revenue, as the paper says.

Why deflate. Without the deflator, a counterfactual that raised a country's nominal wages and prices would appear to raise its pollution even if nothing real changed. Deflating by the price of the input bundle makes emissions homogeneous of degree zero in nominal variables. It also means that emissions follow the resources employed in an industry: a rise in Ti,sT_{i,s}Ti,s​ changes emissions only through the reallocation of resources across industries that it causes, not mechanically. The formula is the model counterpart of equation (14), with Ri,s/ci,sR_{i,s}/c_{i,s}Ri,s​/ci,s​ in the role of sales and γi,s\gamma_{i,s}γi,s​ in the role of intensity. Holding γi,s\gamma_{i,s}γi,s​ fixed in counterfactuals shuts down the technique effect, so the model produces only scale and composition effects.

The first part is exact and uses only equation (21). Write equation (21) in the counterfactual, with γi,s\gamma_{i,s}γi,s​ unchanged, and express each counterfactual variable as its baseline value times its proportional change, Ri,s′=R^i,sRi,sR'_{i,s}=\hat{R}_{i,s}R_{i,s}Ri,s′​=R^i,s​Ri,s​ and ci,s′=c^i,sci,sc'_{i,s}=\hat{c}_{i,s}c_{i,s}ci,s′​=c^i,s​ci,s​:

This is a weighted mean of the changes in real sectoral output, with weights equal to baseline emission shares. Neither γi,s\gamma_{i,s}γi,s​ nor the levels of revenue and cost are needed, only observed emissions and the changes. A sector that is clean at baseline has a small weight, so pollution falls when real output moves from sectors with large emission shares to sectors with small ones, even if total real output rises.

Given baseline shares, revenues, tariffs and deficits, the trade elasticities and the shocks, this system determines the changes in wages, prices, trade shares and revenues up to a numeraire, and R^i,s=Ri,s′/Ri,s\hat{R}_{i,s}=R'_{i,s}/R_{i,s}R^i,s​=Ri,s′​/Ri,s​ then enters the pollution formula.

The mechanism behind the results can be read from these conditions. In the reforming country, industries with Is>0I_s>0Is​>0 have T^i,s>1\hat{T}_{i,s}>1T^i,s​>1 and gain trade shares everywhere, while industries with Is<0I_s<0Is​<0 lose them. The wage is common to all sectors, so c^i,s\hat{c}_{i,s}c^i,s​ differs little across sectors and real output R^i,s/c^i,s\hat{R}_{i,s}/\hat{c}_{i,s}R^i,s​/c^i,s​ rises in dependent industries and falls in the others. Since dependent industries are clean, by equation (2), the sectors with large baseline emission weights contract and E^i<1\hat{\mathcal{E}}_i<1E^i​<1. In other countries T^\hat{T}T^ equals one, but the reforming country's price changes shift their trade shares in the opposite direction, so their dirty sectors expand and their emissions rise. Global emissions change by ∑iEiE^i/∑iEi\sum_i\mathcal{E}_i\hat{\mathcal{E}}_i/\sum_i\mathcal{E}_i∑i​Ei​E^i​/∑i​Ei​, which is small because the changes across countries offset each other.
